groups.label: Code Quality & Guardrails
examples: The 'PR review coverage n/a' / 0.2 reviews-per-PR reading likely understates actual review discipline — every sampled commit message carries a Gerrit Change-Id and most carry a 'Reviewed-on: https://go-review.googlesource.com/...' trailer, direct evidence that changes are reviewed before landing, just not via GitHub's PR mechanism.

The 0% PR-merge / n/a-reviewed-PR figures underlying D6 and D7 likely reflect that this GitHub repo is a mirror of a Gerrit-hosted project (commit messages consistently show Change-Id and 'Reviewed-on: https://go-review.googlesource.com' links) rather than an absence of code review, so the GitHub-PR-based review signal may be structurally blind to this project's actual review mechanism.

The process signal reports 0% reviewed / 0 merged PRs, but every sampled commit message carries a Gerrit `Change-Id` and a `Reviewed-on: https://go-review.googlesource.com` trailer, indicating these changes were actually code-reviewed via Gerrit — the GitHub PR-based detector can't see that off-platform review process and likely understates real review discipline.

The 0% PR-merge-rate and 0.1 reviews/PR figures (feeding D6/D7) likely reflect that GitHub PRs against golang/go are conventionally closed by a bot pointing contributors to Gerrit rather than merged directly on GitHub, so these process metrics probably understate actual review/merge activity rather than indicating an inactive or unreviewed project.

groups.label: Documentation & Knowledge
examples: The D5 signal only credits README.md and CONTRIBUTING.md, but the sampled bpf/doc.go shows a substantial godoc-style package comment explaining the BPF VM model in depth — in-code documentation depth appears understated by a detector focused on top-level markdown files.

The D5 signal (40, based on README + CONTRIBUTING.md alone) may undercount total documentation depth, since CONTRIBUTING.md explicitly references a separate gopls/doc/contributing.md guide, implying at least one additional documentation file/directory not reflected in the reported '3-section README' count.

The D5 signal credits only the root README (score 30), but several subdirectories (gotypes, hello, outyet, appengine-hello, slog-handler-guide) ship their own README files — some generated by the repo's own `weave` doc-generation tool per gotypes/gen.go's go:generate directive — suggesting broader per-package documentation coverage than a single-README signal implies.

groups.label: Automated Testing
examples: Two of the four sampled '_test.go' files (helper_test.go with `// +build OMIT`, final_test.go with `//go:build ignore`) are blog-post illustration snippets deliberately excluded from normal compilation, not active tests, so the D2 signal's file/assertion counts likely overstate the size and rigor of the real automated test suite.

D2 reported 'No test files detected,' but sampled files include vendor/cmd/go/go_test.go, go_unix_test.go, go_windows_test.go, and vendor/cmd/go/internal/cache/cache_test.go — a real, substantial Go test suite is present, even though it's vendored code rather than tests authored by this repo.

The D2 signal (73) may understate real testing rigor — fuzz_test.go shows a native go test -fuzz target (FuzzReader) exercising archive/tar round-trips, which the rubric explicitly calls out as an advanced-rigor signal, and it's unclear the 73 score credits this fuzz-testing evidence.

groups.label: Commit & Velocity Signals
examples: D7 reports 'AI/bot-attributed commits present (5 of 30)', but the sampled commit messages attribute bot involvement to CI automation (e.g. 'Co-authored-by: GitHub <noreply@github.com>' on a scheduled go-version-matrix update), not to an AI coding assistant like Claude or Copilot — this dimension may be overcounting genuine AI-authorship signal.

groups.label: CI/CD & Delivery
examples: The 0/100 'no CI pipeline detected' score may be a visibility blind spot rather than a true absence: golang/go's GitHub presence is a mirror of the canonical Gerrit-hosted repo, and this project's actual build/test verification is known to run through infrastructure outside GitHub Actions, which a GitHub-scoped CI detector cannot see.
